strengths: Identifies and systematically documents a previously overlooked failure mode of unlearning methods: even when forgotten information is explicitly re-supplied in the prompt, unlearned models often fail to use it correctly, producing hallucinations or degenerate text. This is a genuinely useful new evaluation axis (Contextual QA) that complements the standard Direct QA/retain-utility protocol.

The proposed fix (a KL-consistency term anchoring the unlearned model's contextual output distribution to the original model's) is simple, modular, and plugs into multiple existing objectives (RMU, NPO, UNDIAL) with minimal changes, which increases its practical applicability.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation: two models (Gemma-2B-IT, Qwen3-8B), three forget ratios (1/5/10%), six baseline unlearning methods for the diagnostic study, and three methods extended with the context-aware term, evaluated with both ROUGE-L and an LLM-judge metric.

Useful ablations: sensitivity to the new hyperparameter λc (showing robustness across a wide range), robustness of the fix to paraphrased and reasoning-based context variants (not just verbatim context), and consistency of findings across forget-set sizes.
Clear qualitative case studies that make the failure mode and the fix intuitive and convincing to a reader beyond aggregate numbers.
weaknesses: All experiments are conducted solely on the synthetic TOFU benchmark (fictitious author profiles). It is unclear whether the findings and the proposed fix generalize to more realistic unlearning settings (e.g., MUSE, WMDP, real PII/copyright removal), which involve different types of knowledge and different risk profiles.

The paper does not discuss an important tension: for privacy/compliance-motivated unlearning (e.g., outdated regulations), restoring contextual utility is desirable, but for safety-motivated unlearning (e.g., WMDP-style hazardous knowledge removal), enabling the model to readily use forgotten dangerous information when it appears in context could be undesirable or even harmful. This limitation is not acknowledged, which weakens the generality of the claimed contribution.

The convergence/epoch-selection procedure and the λc selection both rely on identifying the epoch/hyperparameter that jointly maximizes Contextual QA and utility while matching Direct QA to the vanilla baseline within a tolerance — this is essentially oracle model selection on the same test metrics being reported, raising concerns about optimistic bias in the reported numbers; no held-out validation split or blind stopping rule is used.

Evaluation relies on a single LLM judge (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) with binary scoring and no human validation of judge reliability, and no variance/seed-based statistics are reported, limiting confidence in the precision of the reported gains.
Model scale is limited to 2B and 8B parameter instruction-tuned models; it is unclear whether the phenomenon and fix hold at larger scales or for base (non-instruction-tuned) models.

The context-aware term requires constructing paired forget-QA-with-context examples for training, which adds a data-curation requirement not present in vanilla unlearning baselines; the paper does not discuss the cost/effort of constructing such context pairs in real deployment settings or how sensitive the results are to the quality/coverage of these context pairs.

The method itself (KL-regularization to preserve a desired behavior) is a fairly standard/incremental technique borrowed directly from RLHF-style alignment; the core novelty lies more in the diagnostic framing than in the technical mechanism.

strengths: Identifies a genuinely underexplored and practically relevant evaluation axis for LLM unlearning -- whether models can still use forgotten knowledge when it reappears in the prompt/RAG context -- and shows convincingly that six widely-used unlearning methods degrade this ability, sometimes to near zero.
The proposed fix (a KL-consistency term anchoring contextual predictions to the original model) is simple, modular, and easy to integrate into existing objectives with minimal changes.

Fairly extensive empirical protocol: two models (Gemma-2B-IT, Qwen3-8B), three forget ratios, per-epoch tracking, qualitative case studies, and an ablation on the new hyperparameter lambda_c showing it is not overly sensitive.
The additional 'robustness to context variants' study (paraphrase, reasoning-based context) is a nice touch that goes beyond verbatim context matching.
Clear writing, well-organized figures, and a coherent narrative connecting the diagnosis (Section 3) to the fix (Section 4-5).
weaknesses: Fundamental conceptual tension is left unaddressed: the paper's own motivating scenario is removing 'sensitive information' or PII, yet the proposed method explicitly restores the model's ability to reason over and reproduce that exact content once it is supplied in context. For privacy/compliance-driven unlearning (the stated use case in the intro), this could be actively counterproductive or even risky (e.g., re-surfacing sensitive PII when pasted back by any user), and the paper never discusses this trade-off or when contextual utility is/ isn't desirable.

All experiments are confined to the synthetic TOFU benchmark (fictitious author profiles). There is no evaluation on more realistic unlearning benchmarks (e.g., MUSE, WMDP, real-world PII/copyright removal tasks) where the dynamics of memorization, context use, and safety risk differ substantially from fictitious facts never seen in pretraining.

Model scale is limited to a 2B and an 8B model; no evidence is given that the contextual-suppression phenomenon or the proposed fix generalizes to larger, more capable LLMs that are more commonly deployed in production RAG systems.

The core technical contribution -- a KL term aligning outputs with the frozen original model on contextual queries -- is a fairly direct adaptation of standard RLHF-style regularization and is technically modest; no comparison is made against simpler baselines (e.g., simply adding contextual QA pairs with the gold answer into the retain-set fine-tuning loss, or standard supervised fine-tuning on S^ctx_f) to establish that the KL-based formulation is actually necessary rather than any form of contextual data inclusion.

Only 3 of the 6 evaluated unlearning methods (NPO, RMU, UNDIAL) are extended with the context-aware objective; DPO, GradAscent, and GradDiff, which showed some of the worst contextual degradation in Section 3, are never tested with the proposed fix, leaving open whether the approach generalizes across the full space of unlearning objectives.

LLM-Judge evaluation relies solely on a single model (Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2) with binary scoring and no reported inter-rater agreement, human validation, or discussion of judge bias/robustness, which is a concern given that most of the paper's headline numbers are LLM-Judge scores.

No variance/multiple-seed reporting; all numbers appear to be single-run results, making it hard to assess whether the reported gains (e.g., +0.90 LLM-Judge for RMU) are robust or subject to run-to-run variability, especially given the noisy, sometimes degenerate outputs seen in the qualitative examples (e.g., RMU vanilla producing 'sb sb sb...' gibberish).

The convergence/epoch-selection procedure (picking the epoch within tolerance of best Direct/Contextual/Utility scores, with a further delta-tolerance for selecting lambda_c) is somewhat ad hoc and could implicitly favor the proposed method if the selection criteria are not applied with equal rigor to the vanilla baselines, raising minor concerns about fairness of the comparison.
No discussion of computational/memory overhead from computing the extra KL term and maintaining a frozen reference model copy during training, which is relevant for practical adoption claims.

strengths: Identifies a genuinely useful and previously overlooked blind spot in LLM unlearning evaluation: that current methods, while suppressing direct recall, also cripple the model's ability to use the very same (forgotten) information when it is re-supplied in context (e.g., via RAG). This is well-motivated with realistic use cases (e.g., outdated regulations re-introduced for historical comparison).

The empirical study in Section 3 is systematic and convincing: six unlearning methods, two model families (Gemma-2B-IT, Qwen3-8B), three forget ratios, tracked across 20 training epochs with both ROUGE-L and LLM-Judge metrics, consistently showing large drops in Contextual QA performance (up to 100% relative degradation) even when the correct answer is given verbatim in the prompt.

The proposed fix (adding a KL-consistency term against the frozen original model's contextual distribution) is simple, clearly motivated, and modular -- it can be layered onto any existing two-term unlearning objective with minimal changes.

Strong, consistent empirical gains when applying the augmentation to three representative methods (RMU, NPO, UNDIAL): Contextual QA LLM-Judge scores rise to near-ceiling (≥0.95) in nearly all configurations, while Direct QA forgetting and retain-set utility remain largely unchanged (within a few percentage points).

Useful supporting ablations: sensitivity to forget-set ratio (1/5/10%), sensitivity/robustness to the λc hyperparameter (showing the method is easy to tune), and robustness to paraphrased/reasoning-based context variants rather than only verbatim context.
Clear qualitative case studies that make the failure modes and fixes tangible (e.g., RMU producing gibberish vs. context-aware RMU recovering the correct fact).
weaknesses: All experiments are conducted solely on the synthetic TOFU benchmark (fictitious author profiles). It remains unclear whether the phenomenon and the proposed fix generalize to more realistic unlearning settings involving real sensitive/copyrighted/PII data or benchmarks like MUSE or WMDP, where contextual re-exposure has very different stakes.

The paper does not adequately engage with a central tension it creates: making unlearned models highly responsive to forgotten content when it reappears in context could make them more vulnerable to context-based knowledge-extraction or jailbreak attacks (a concern the related work section itself cites via Shumailov et al. and Cooper et al.). There is no discussion or experiment addressing whether restoring near-perfect contextual utility undermines the privacy/compliance guarantees that motivate unlearning in the first place (e.g., an adversary supplying a plausible-looking but partially wrong 'context' to fish for the real fact).

The technical contribution is a fairly direct application of KL-regularization (as used in RLHF/PPO-style alignment) to a new auxiliary objective; the core novelty of the paper lies more in the evaluation/diagnosis than in algorithmic innovation.

Only two model backbones (2B and 8B parameters) are tested, both relatively small; it is unclear whether the same suppression phenomenon and fix hold at larger scales or for different architectures/instruction-tuning recipes.

The context-aware augmentation is only evaluated on 3 of the 6 originally studied methods (RMU, NPO, UNDIAL), omitting GradDiff, DPO, and GradAscent, which showed some of the worst contextual degradation in Section 3 — leaving open whether the fix generalizes to those objectives.

Evaluation relies on a single LLM judge (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) with binary scoring and no reported human validation or inter-rater reliability, and results appear to be single-run (no variance/seed reporting), making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the reported gains.

The λc selection procedure (grid search + picking the best point matching vanilla forgetting within a tolerance δ) is somewhat post-hoc; while the paper argues robustness across λc values, the main reported numbers reflect a tuned best case rather than a fixed, principled default.
No explicit Limitations section; broader risks (e.g., dual-use concerns from restoring contextual utility) and scope restrictions (TOFU-only, model scale) are not clearly consolidated for the reader.

strengths: Identifies a novel and practically important evaluation gap in LLM unlearning research: whether unlearned models can still correctly use forgotten information when it is explicitly reintroduced as context (e.g., via RAG or user-supplied documents). This is a realistic and underexplored scenario given the prevalence of context-augmented LLM usage.

Extensive empirical evaluation: six unlearning methods (plus four additional baselines in the appendix), two models of different scale/architecture (Gemma-2B-IT, Qwen3-8B), two datasets (TOFU and the relationally entangled PISTOL), multiple forget ratios (1/5/10%), and multiple metrics (ROUGE-L, LLM-Judge, token accuracy, ChrF).

The proposed fix (a KL-consistency term anchoring contextual predictions to the frozen original model) is simple, modular, and plugs into diverse existing objectives (gradient-based, preference-based, representation-based) with minimal modification, and is shown to be robust to a wide range of the weighting hyperparameter λc.

Thorough robustness analysis beyond the clean verbatim-context setting: paraphrased contexts, reasoning-based contexts, long/noisy GPT-generated paragraphs, and mixed contexts with conflicting distractors (up to 5), showing the method's benefits persist under realistic degradation of context quality.
Human-agreement validation of the LLM-Judge metric (Cohen's κ ≈ 0.95) lends some credibility to the automatic evaluation protocol.
Clear qualitative case studies (Tables 1, 3, 4) that vividly illustrate the failure mode (e.g., RMU degenerating into repeated tokens) and the fix, complementing the quantitative results.
Reasonably honest limitations section acknowledging model-scale constraints and forgetting/contextual-utility trade-offs.
weaknesses: Experiments are limited to relatively small models (2B and 8B parameters); it is unclear whether the observed contextual-suppression phenomenon and the proposed fix generalize to larger, production-scale LLMs where representational capacity and unlearning dynamics may differ substantially.

The primary benchmark (TOFU) uses synthetic fictitious author profiles; despite the PISTOL extension, external validity to the paper's motivating real-world scenarios (copyrighted book chapters, personal income records) is not directly demonstrated.

The paper does not clearly test whether unlearning also degrades Contextual QA performance on the retain set (non-forgotten entities), which would help determine whether the phenomenon is a forget-specific side effect versus a more general erosion of in-context/instruction-following ability caused by fine-tuning-based unlearning; this ambiguity affects the interpretation of the core claim.

Some reported "marginal" forgetting/utility trade-offs are non-trivial in relative terms (e.g., RMU's Direct QA ROUGE-L roughly triples from 0.04 to 0.13 after adding the context-aware term), which slightly undercuts the claim that forgetting is fully preserved; a more careful discussion of when/why this degradation occurs would strengthen the paper.
No variance/error bars or multiple-seed reporting is provided for the main results, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the (often large) reported deltas.

The method requires access to a frozen copy of the pre-unlearning model as a reference for the KL term, which increases memory/compute overhead relative to vanilla unlearning and may not always be feasible in strict compliance settings; this cost is only briefly addressed in the appendix.

Limited discussion of potential dual-use/adversarial implications: explicitly training the model to trust and reproduce content matching forgotten information when given as context could, in principle, ease adversarial extraction of forgotten data via crafted or partially-true contexts, and this risk is not directly analyzed despite the robustness experiments being suggestive.

strengths: Identifies a real and underexplored evaluation gap in LLM unlearning research: whether unlearned models can still correctly use the forgotten information when it is explicitly reintroduced as context, which is highly relevant to RAG and user-document deployment scenarios.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad: six unlearning methods, two model families (Gemma-2B-IT, Qwen3-8B), three forget ratios, the TOFU and PISTOL benchmarks, additional baselines (DPO, GradDiff, PDU, SimNPO), and several robustness probes (paraphrased contexts, noisy GPT-generated contexts, mixed/conflicting-distractor contexts).
A human-agreement study (Cohen's kappa ~0.95) lends some credibility to the LLM-Judge metric used throughout.
The proposed KL-consistency context term is simple, modular, and shown to be relatively insensitive to its weighting hyperparameter, which is a practically useful property.
Qualitative case studies (Tables 1, 3, 4) make the failure mode and the proposed fix intuitively clear.
weaknesses: The proposed fix essentially continues training the model directly on contextual QA data drawn from the forget set with the exact same template used at evaluation time (Figure 3, Section 4.2). This raises a serious circularity/overfitting concern: near-perfect Contextual QA scores (0.97–0.99) may largely reflect the model learning to copy/use information when it appears in this specific templated format, rather than a genuine, robust restoration of contextual grounding. The robustness experiments (noisy, mixed-context) partially address this, but performance degrades substantially in harder settings (e.g., RMU context-aware drops to 0.34–0.36 LLM-Judge with 4–5 distractors, and 0.605 under long/noisy context vs. near-perfect scores under verbatim context), suggesting the gains are template-sensitive rather than a general fix.

The core technical contribution is incremental: nearly all unlearning objectives already contain a retain-term-style regularizer toward the original/reference model; adding a third KL term anchored on contextual examples is a natural and fairly small extension rather than a conceptually new mechanism. The paper's theoretical justification for why this works (Section 4.2) is largely qualitative/hand-wavy, without formal analysis connecting the representation-level claims to the fix.

No comparison against simpler/obvious baselines, e.g., simply increasing the existing retain-term weight, fine-tuning on contextual QA examples without any forget objective, or using a generic ICL/robustness-tuning dataset unrelated to the specific forget set — making it hard to isolate whether the gains come from the proposed context-aware mechanism specifically or just from additional targeted fine-tuning on the forget set's contextual form.

Benchmarks are limited to synthetic, templated datasets (TOFU fictitious authors, PISTOL synthetic contracts) with short, formulaic QA pairs; it is unclear whether findings and the proposed fix generalize to realistic unlearning targets such as actual copyrighted text or naturally occurring PII with more complex, free-form language.
Model scale is limited to 2B and 8B parameters; no evidence is given that the phenomenon or the fix generalizes to larger, more capable models increasingly used in production.

The hyperparameter selection procedure for λc (grid search + convergence criteria + an arbitrary tolerance δ=0.06 for matching vanilla forgetting) is somewhat ad hoc and could bias the reported comparisons in the method's favor.

The paper does not seriously grapple with the tension it creates for compliance use-cases: strengthening a model's ability to reproduce forgotten PII/copyrighted content when supplied in context could itself be viewed as a compliance risk in settings where any reproduction of the protected content (even from user-supplied context) is undesirable; this is only superficially addressed in the Limitations section.
Figures (e.g., Figure 4, Figure 9) are dense with many overlapping curves across methods and ratios, which reduces interpretability despite informative content.

strengths: Identifies and names a genuinely underexplored failure mode of LLM unlearning—'contextual utility'—the inability of unlearned models to correctly use forgotten information when it is explicitly reintroduced in the prompt. This is a practically important blind spot in existing Direct-QA-only evaluation protocols (e.g., TOFU, MUSE).

The empirical demonstration that six widely used unlearning methods (GradAscent, GradDiff, DPO, NPO, RMU, UNDIAL) all substantially degrade Contextual QA performance, sometimes to near zero (e.g., RMU LLM-Judge < 0.05), is clear, consistent across two models (Gemma-2B-IT, Qwen3-8B) and three forget ratios, and reinforced with convincing qualitative case studies showing degenerate or hallucinated outputs even when the correct answer is given verbatim in context.

The proposed fix—a modular KL-consistency term anchoring contextual predictions to the frozen original model—is simple, theoretically well-motivated (clear mechanistic explanation in Section 4.1/Appendix A.5 of why forget-term penalties leak into contextual representations), and easy to plug into existing objectives with minimal modification.

Extensive and careful experimental validation: results across two model scales, three forget ratios, a second dataset (PISTOL) with structurally entangled entities, additional baselines (DPO, GradDiff, PDU, SimNPO), additional metrics (token accuracy, ChrF), hyperparameter sensitivity analysis showing robustness to λc, and stress tests under noisy/long contexts and multi-distractor conflicting contexts—this breadth substantially strengthens the soundness of the claims.
Reasonable attention to reproducibility and evaluation validity, including a human-agreement study for the LLM-Judge metric (Cohen's κ = 0.95) and full prompt templates in the appendix.
Honest limitations section acknowledging the forgetting/contextual-utility trade-off and the restriction to models up to 8B parameters and two benchmarks.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to the synthetic TOFU benchmark (fictitious authors) and the PISTOL dataset; both are relatively narrow, templated QA settings. It remains unclear how well the findings and the proposed fix generalize to natural pretraining-scale memorized content, longer-form generation, or multi-hop/real-world factual knowledge where 'ground-truth context' is not as cleanly delineated.

Model scale is limited to 2B and 8B parameters; given that contextual grounding behavior can change substantially with scale and instruction-tuning strength, it is uncertain whether the degradation phenomenon and the proposed remedy hold for larger, more capable models actually deployed in production.

The context-aware objective requires constructing paired (question, context, answer) triples for the forget set and retaining a frozen copy of the original model for KL supervision; this assumes access to clean, fully correct contextual exemplars for every forget item, which may not always be available in realistic unlearning requests (e.g., when ground-truth context itself is ambiguous or unavailable).

The robustness analysis to paraphrased/reasoning-based/noisy contexts is based on a single qualitative case study (Table 4) for the main robustness claim, while the more systematic noisy/mixed-context experiments (Appendix A.10–A.11) are only conducted for Gemma-2B-IT, leaving generalization to the larger model and to more diverse context types less verified.

Because the fix essentially distills the unlearned model's contextual behavior back toward the original (pre-unlearning) model, there is limited discussion of potential residual leakage risk—e.g., whether an adversary could exploit the contextual pathway to partially reconstruct forgotten knowledge through creatively crafted or partially-correct contexts, beyond the limited paraphrase/reasoning case study.

The paper's theoretical grounding for why the context term fixes the suppression is primarily intuitive/qualitative (Section 4.2, Appendix A.5) rather than formally analyzed; the claim of 'stability and insensitivity to λc' would benefit from more rigorous justification beyond empirical curves for one model.
